speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: The Committee was set up by the honourable Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon in August 2016 to conduct a root-and-branch review of the professional training regime for lawyers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: This review was aimed at raising the quality and consistency of training standards across the industry.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: The Committee was chaired by Justice Quentin Loh and comprised 14 other members including representatives from the Supreme Court, the Attorney-General's Chambers, the Ministry of Law (MinLaw), the Law Society of Singapore, the Singapore Corporate Counsel Association and various Singapore law practices.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: A working group comprising representatives from MinLaw, the Singapore Institute of Legal Education (SILE), the Supreme Court and the Law Society of Singapore was subsequently set up to implement and operationalise the Committee's recommendations, which my Ministry had accepted in-principle.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: A separate working group was established by the SILE to implement the Committee's recommendations on Part B and practice training.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: This working group comprises representatives from the SILE's Board, Singapore law practices, the three local law schools, the Law Society, the Singapore Academy of Law, the Singapore Corporate Counsel Association, the Attorney-General's Chambers and MinLaw.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: In 2019, MinLaw conducted a public consultation on the working group's proposals for implementing the Committee's recommendations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: I will now cover each of the key amendments in turn.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: The rest of the Committee's recommendations will be implemented progressively via guidance notes and industry announcements, in consultation with the relevant stakeholders from the working group.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: I will start with the amendment in relation to decoupling admission to the Singapore Bar from the completion of practice training contracts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: The existing framework for admission to the Singapore Bar as an Advocate and Solicitor (A&S) requires law graduates to, amongst other requirements, pass Part B of the Singapore Bar Examinations (the Part B examinations) and complete a prescribed practice training period.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: During the practice training period, the law graduate receives supervised training in relation to the practice of Singapore law under a formal training arrangement.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: This formal training arrangement between a law graduate and a Singapore law practice is known as a "practice training contract".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Clause 6 of the Bill introduces a new category of individuals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Such a lawyer (NP) may be admitted as an A&S and will have the rights and obligations of one after the completion of the prescribed practice training period.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: This enhancement to the admission framework recognises that a legal education can lead to different legal career pathways.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: MinLaw remains focused on developing a strong core of practising lawyers to serve Singapore's society and to provide high quality legal services to enhance our business environment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: However, our reality is one of a fast-changing operating environment and we need legal talent to support all aspects of our economy and society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Law graduates can join in-house counsel teams, legal tech companies or enter academia.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: They can contribute to the legal services sector and in other sectors which may benefit from legal expertise in a variety of roles and functions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: For those who do not intend to practise, this change allows them to be admitted to the Singapore Bar earlier, since they do not need to complete practice training.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: This also frees up more practice training contracts for those who intend to practise law.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: As highlighted in the Forward SG report, one of our shared visions is to embrace a wider variety of career pathways.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: We are committed to recognising that there are diverse pathways that are available for our lawyers to develop their full potential.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Hence, this change will allow law graduates who do not wish to practise to embark on their chosen career pathways sooner.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: A lawyer (NP)’s rights and obligations will be similar to a non-practising A&S who does not have in force a Practising Certificate (PC).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: For example, lawyers (NP) may work as in-house counsel and may provide pro bono or free legal advice.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: They will also be members of the Singapore Academy of Law and be members of the Law Society of Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Lawyers (NP) will also be officers of the court, like A&Ses today, and subject to the disciplinary oversight of the Courts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Furthermore, under Clause 16 of the Bill, a lawyer (NP) who is employed by a law practice, but is not a practice trainee and who does not have a provisional PC, may be registered as a regulated non-practitioner under section 36G of the Act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Such registration will be subject to the prevailing framework for regulated non-practitioners, including being entitled to be a director, partner or shareholder of a law firm or similar entity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: I will elaborate on provisional PCs later on.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Similarly, the Bill will also permit non-practising A&Ses to be registered as regulated non-practitioners, subject to the prevailing requirements.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: This acknowledges that an individual who is admitted to the Singapore Bar, can contribute to a law practice even if he or she does not practise.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: While this change will be given effect to via upcoming amendments to the subsidiary legislation, I would like to mention this briefly, so that Members have an overall picture of the changes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: This change is only one example of consistent efforts to holistically lift the standards of the legal industry.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: My Ministry is also involved in ongoing reviews in other aspects covering areas such as legal education, and ethics and professional standards of lawyers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: These reviews aim to enhance the quality of the legal workforce and complement the Committee’s recommendations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: In an increasingly complex and competitive operating environment, there is a greater demand for legal professionals that provide high-quality advice and solutions to clients with multi-faceted problems.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: One key objective is to produce law graduates who will be equipped with the necessary skill sets and be better prepared to enter into the legal workforce.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: In conjunction with these efforts, the lengthened practice training period will: give practice trainees a longer period of direct mentorship to develop a strong foundation for a sustainable and fulfilling career in legal practice; better equip practice trainees for entry into private practice through greater exposure to a range of practice areas; and allow law practices to make a more holistic assessment of trainees’ performance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: In other jurisdictions like France, Germany and Hong Kong, there is also emphasis on the practice training to complement formal education where solicitors are required to undergo two years of training.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: The SILE has published a detailed Notice on New Admission Regime on their website.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: The Notice captures the proposals from the multi-stakeholder working groups.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: It outlines the new training requirements and options available to law graduates seeking to complete their practice training period.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: MinLaw is aware of industry concerns surrounding the lengthened practice training period, including the additional strain this may place on both future practice trainees and law practices seeking to offer practice training contracts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: MinLaw is working closely with the SILE and the Law Society on these concerns.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Areas that we are looking into include arrangements for leave days and medical leave, and renumeration for practice trainees commensurate with their contributions during their training period.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Another amendment relates to providing trainees the option to practise provisionally under supervision.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Clause 12 introduces a framework for “Provisional Practising Certificates”, or provisional PC.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: This will replace the existing “part-call” regime, which only permits practice trainees to have restricted rights of audience to appear and plead before the Courts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: The provisional PC provides exposure to a broader variety of experiences that more closely reflect the realities and rigours of private practice.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: This will contribute to building a stronger foundation for young lawyers who are starting their legal careers and can provide a smoother transition to independent practice.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Clause 12 also sets out the power of the Attorney-General, the Registrar of the Supreme Court, and the Council of the Law Society of Singapore in respect of the issue of provisional PCs and the imposition of any further conditions thereof.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: It also sets out when an application for a provisional PC may be refused, and when a provisional PC may be suspended or cancelled.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Provision is also made for appeals against the Registrar’s decisions in provisional PC applications, and to introduce measures concerning a lawyer (NP)’s fitness to practise provisionally and when a lawyer (NP) is disqualified from applying for a provisional PC.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: These are substantively similar to the corresponding provisions in the LPA concerning PCs and A&Ses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: This expands the training options for practice trainees and can add to their breadth of practical and commercial experience, so that they are better able to meet the needs of the businesses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: The SILE, in consultation with the working group, is working through the applicable criteria.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: These criteria will be prescribed in the subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: A further amendment relates to the moratorium for practice training contract applications.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: At present, the search for practice training contracts is highly competitive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: MinLaw has received feedback that law students feel pressured to start competing with their peers for practice training contracts from as early as their first year in law school.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: This would alleviate the law students’ anxieties in the practice training contract application process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Further details on the moratorium’s implementation will be announced in due course.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: This includes when the moratorium will be introduced, its duration, the relevant criteria for compliance, and the consequences of any breach.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: The Bill amends the Act to provide flexibility to implement these details in the future.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: The next set of amendments relate to interim disciplinary provisions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Clauses 25 provides that lawyers (NP) are officers of the Supreme Court.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Just like A&Ses, lawyers (NP) will be subject to the disciplinary proceedings framework in Part 7 of the Act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: In this regard, MinLaw is currently conducting a broader review of the Act’s disciplinary proceedings framework as a whole, with a view towards further legislative amendments in the future.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: This review takes into account recent developments in the case law, as well as feedback from various stakeholders on the Act’s existing provisions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: In doing so, MinLaw aims to ensure that the law is clear, that disciplinary proceedings against lawyers are conducted expeditiously and fairly, and that the Act continues to engender public trust in the legal profession.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Members who are lawyers will appreciate how the Act’s various discipline-related provisions are inter-connected.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: MinLaw will require more time to complete the review, including consulting relevant stakeholders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: In the meantime, clauses 26 to 31 of the Bill insert interim provisions for the discipline of lawyers (NP).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: These interim provisions are based on today’s existing provisions for the discipline of non-practising A&Ses, practice trainees and “part-called” individuals, with adjustments where appropriate.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: The substance of these interim provisions are subject to change, pending the completion of the review.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: The amendment at clause 48 of the Bill contains transitional arrangements to implement the changes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Individuals who became qualified persons before 1 November 2023 may apply for admission to the Singapore Bar under the current admission framework, if they meet the current requirements and apply for admission as an A&S before the 2024 session of the Part B Examinations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: We recognise, however, that some individuals may become qualified persons between 1 November 2023 and 31 January 2024, and are able to complete six months of practice training before the new admission framework is implemented in 2024.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: This Bill also makes miscellaneous and technical amendments to the Act and clarifies certain provisions based on stakeholders’ feedback.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: The first clarifies the Court’s powers in an application to be admitted to the Singapore Bar, after the recent incidents of individuals cheating during the Part B examinations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: The Court may, considering the applicant’s conduct, character and other relevant circumstances: (a)	adjourn the application for a specified period; (b)	allow it to be withdrawn; or (c)	make any other appropriate order.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: The second clarifies that a Court of 3 Supreme Court Judges constituted under the Act may conduct or hear a matter through electronic means, unless otherwise prescribed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Similar amendments pertaining to the Supreme Court, State Courts, and Family Justice Courts were made via the Courts (Civil and Criminal Justice) Reform Act 2021.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: This amendment is clarificatory in nature and does not introduce new powers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: Our operating environment has become more complex and competitive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam) (for Minister for Law)
text: It remains a top priority to empower our law graduates to build themselves a sustainable and fulfilling career, by offering a breadth of opportunities to them in the legal services sector.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It began with the key idea of a reminder to all of us who live under the rule of law – that law is a profession, not an occupation, in that lawyers must strive to serve the public interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As was mentioned by the hon Senior Parliamentary Secretary just now, in 2016, the honourable Chief Justice, established the Committee for the Professional Training of Lawyers (CPTL) headed by the honourable Justice Quentin Loh to “conduct a root-and-branch review of the professional training regime for trainee lawyers”.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some of the drivers for this review were: one, the fast-changing legal environment which required lawyers to work collaboratively over borders; two, the advent of Artificial Intelligence that have the potential to redefine the role of lawyers and the provision of legal services to clients; and three, the increasing savviness of clients; particularly corporate clients.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The focus was to identify, and I quote, "measures to strengthen the entire professional training regime such that the quality of training remains robust”.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is key is that training is not to be understood as merely the development of professional skills.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The CPTL emphasised the need to teach trainees the deeper purpose associated with acquiring the skills.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If law is a profession and if lawyers have a duty to serve the public, then trainees must be imbued with important values such as compassion, courage and commitment to serve justice and integrity.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The honourable the Chief Justice put this point across poignantly in his speech in 2016 when he announced the set-up of CPTL.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His Honour stated as follows, and I quote: “Law is not the only choice for those who have managed to secure a "fistful of "As", as one interview put it to us…If it is the lure of financial rewards that draws you, you should look at other options or be prepared for disappointment." I wish to pick up one point that was left unsaid but, nonetheless, clear to everyone who is familiar with the developments then.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The quality of our lawyers determines the quality of our Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, ensuring the quality of our young lawyers, not just in terms of skills and knowledge but values, will have an impact, over time, on the quality of our Judiciary which, we all recognise, is an important and co-equal pillar in our Westminster-styled Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Maintaining the quality of the Judiciary is a national imperative.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And I need only quote the hon Minister for Law who, in 2018, said in this House: "When the quality of the Judiciary suffers, the rule of law suffers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support these recommendations but have a few queries on the recommendations which I will deal with in turn.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the lengthening of the practice training period, the CPTL, in its report, identified two main reasons to recommend the doubling of the training period.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, they may even be seconded to a company as internal counsel for up to three months.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, it was felt that a six-month period was too short for a trainee to develop an aptitude to deal with the pressures of practice once he/she is called to the bar.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This was, in fact, a point that was raised by junior lawyers in a focus group discussion that CPTL conducted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The CPTL further noted that, from a comparative study, that the training period in Singapore is much shorter than that of barristers and solicitors in the United Kingdom (UK), Hong Kong, Australia and several other countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Quite clearly though, the key outcome we are looking at is not just the length of the training, but the quality of the lawyer who emerges from it.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And this outcome depends largely on the supervising solicitors.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This was a point that was specifically highlighted by the CPTL.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am aware that, already, there is a checklist that the trainees would have to tick off against, to ensure that they get the requisite exposure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also note that the CPTL has made recommendations, such as "training the trainer" courses, designating a "training partner" in firms with six or more lawyers and so on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Furthermore, supervising solicitors' responsibilities are also spelt out under the Legal Profession (Admission) Rules 2011.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Anecdotally, there are cases of trainees not getting the requisite exposure from their supervising solicitors.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, they are naturally concerned about the possible impact on their own career should they raise issue about such matters to their firm.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would be grateful for the hon Senior Parliamentary Secretary's response to this matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, Sir, the practice trainees who are subscribed to longer training periods, will naturally be concerned about their remuneration for this extended period.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Instead of getting lawyers' salaries, they will continue to get allowances for an extended period.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will mean that law practices will have to incur higher costs, should they increase the allowances to be paid to practice trainees.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The CPTL encouraged a review of this position, so that law practices will be able to defray the costs associated with a longer practice training period.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is not a matter of making profits for the firms, but really a point of fairness – if the trainees are doing work that add value to the client, the client should be willing to pay for it and the firm should be allowed to charge.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The key is to create such a market with full transparency.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, on CPTL's recommendation that the standard and stringency of the Part B examinations be raised, I understand that this is an issue that is receiving the attention of the Singapore Institute of Legal Education, which is a Statutory Board set up under the LPA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I accept that the standards of the Bar exam must be sufficiently high to ensure that persons who pass, have an adequate standard of academic quality.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the other hand, we must guard against the tendency to make the Bar exam harder than necessary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Otherwise, our young talents will miss the chance of being developed into lawyers and, ultimately, Singapore will be the loser.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have also noted some disquiet, expressed particularly in the social media amongst persons sitting for the Part B exam, who noted that the breadth of subjects being introduced for the Part B course are very wide and include specialist law areas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In addition, there is a concern that bell curve grading will be introduced for Part B exams.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I seek the hon Senior Parliamentary Secretary's views on how it is proposed that a proper balance be struck in these circumstances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Here, we must be clear about the specific outcome that we want to achieve – it is not whether the 99% pass rate, on its own, is too high, or that 70% is too low.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is whether law graduates who pass the Part B examinations will be lawyers who can stand shoulder-to-shoulder with lawyers across the world and possess the competence to discharge their responsibilities well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On CPTL's third structural recommendation of uncoupling the admission to bar from completion of practice training contracts, I have an observation to make.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that it is proposed that a non-practicing lawyer, in addition to be being admitted to the Roll of Lawyers, be also members of the Law Society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Notwithstanding that they can be members of the Law Society, only practitioner members may be elected to the Council of the Law Society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am aware that there are other professional bodies which allow non-practising members to be elected into their respective councils.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my respectful view, given the unique duties of the Law Society as set out under the LPA, it is correct to continue to rely on practitioner members, with the requisite knowledge and experience, to be responsible for managing the affairs of the Law Society and ensuring that the Society discharges its statutory functions under the LPA properly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Nonetheless, given that it is now to be statutorily provided that non-practicing lawyers may be Law Society members, there will be a need for the Law Society to cater to their interests too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In addition, there is an opportunity for the Law Society to harness the energies and abilities of these new members in discharging its responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I express the hope that the Law Society members from all categories will be able to work together for the collective good of the legal community and, of course, our country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now deal with the miscellaneous amendments proposed in the Bill on the process issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, I turn to the proposal to issue practice trainees with provisional practicing certificates, authorising him or her to practise provisionally after they have served six months of traineeship.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that the intention is to allow the practice trainee to do anything that an advocate and solicitor can do, provided that they are under the supervision of a supervising solicitor.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The period of coverage is not just during the practice training period, but also after the training period, but before he or she is admitted as an advocate and solicitor.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, advocates and solicitors, before they can apply for a practising certificate, will have to take out a malpractice insurance under the Legal Profession (Professional Indemnity Insurance) Rules.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If not, what steps will be put in place to ensure that there is an indemnity insurance in place, covering civil liability arising from the acts or omissions of practice trainees with provisional practicing certificates?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, would law practices be required to pay extra premiums as a result of this arrangement?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, and finally, I turn to professional training of Judicial Service or Legal Service Officers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, different training periods apply to law graduates who seek admission to the Bar by working as an officer in judicial service, legal service or the Public Defender's Office.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How we train lawyers cannot be a mere technicality or a mere process of mastering the practice of law, but must be a careful and continuous appreciation of the solemn obligations placed on all lawyers, as officers of the Court, to uphold the rule of law and conduct themselves as members of an honourable profession.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, could the hon Senior Parliamentary Secretary clarify what exactly a lawyer (NP), who is not pursuing a practice training, is qualified to do.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, would the lawyer (NP) designation be the required minimum, in order for a person to be an in-house legal counsel in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The lawyer (NP) designation may also confuse members of the public as to whether these persons are able to provide legal advice or to act legally for them, which remains the preserve of advocates and solicitors holding a practicing certificate.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I urge the Ministry to take steps to ensure public communications to equip members of the public to be able to tell the difference.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I support the spirit of this move, as it would give aspiring advocates and solicitors good exposure to the work in corporations that would contribute to a more well-rounded training experience.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: However, could the hon Senior Parliamentary Secretary provide some clarity on the approval process for these corporations and in-house legal departments?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, could the hon Senior Parliamentary Secretary also clarify how lawyers (NP), and the law firms they are training with, would have access to these three-month attachments?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Would the approved corporations have the ability to choose which trainees to accept?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And I hope that the system will ensure fair access to trainees from all firms: small, medium and large.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We should avoid a system where trainees at larger firms have a higher chance of being involved in these attachments, just by virtue of being at these firms, and those from smaller firms are being prejudiced.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Third, I would like to ask if the hon Senior Parliamentary Secretary could provide some clarity on how the moratorium for practice training contract applications, also to be given effect by subsidiary legislation, would operate.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The longer training period means that law firms that take on trainees will not be likely to charge for their trainees' work for a longer duration.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Clients of smaller firms, with generally tighter budgets, may not be amendable to paying for trainees' time, costs or for their work, although their new designation of lawyer (NP) may be persuasive to some extent.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, could the hon Senior Parliamentary Secretary give some clarity as to whether the time and cost of trainees could be charged to clients?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, with a longer training period, trainees may expect higher allowances, because their higher full-time fee earner salaries will be pushed back now by six months.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This may be difficult for smaller law firms to swallow.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As I mentioned earlier, the three-month attachments, as part of a training practice contract, could also end up being prejudicial to smaller law firms, if the corporations can and do pick primarily brand name law firms from which to accept trainees.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This House has made several changes, including those before the House today, to the legal profession over the past few years, in order to position the industry for the future.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These changes must not only benefit the 3% of large firms, but also help to unlock the latent value in the other 97% which would significantly increase the overall value add of the legal industry to the Singapore economy.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I trust that the Ministry will continue to ensure that the benefits of the changes to the profession are equally accessible by lawyers in smaller firms as well as in large firms.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I too have a few queries on the amendment Bill for the Senior Parliamentary Secretary.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: First is the length of time to qualify to be a practising lawyer.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This means that in future, any aspiring lawyer would now have to undergo four years of academic study to obtain a law degree, spend six months preparing for the Part B examination and then spend one year on a practice training period – a total of five-and-a-half years.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For an aspiring lawyer who comes from a poor family, the additional six months on a practice training contract would impose additional financial constraint on the family.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It may also deter those who have the right attitude, skillset or talent from taking up law as a career because of the length of time required.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For some students, a delay in six months may mean nothing.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But for a law student from a poorer background, that delay of six months would mean an inability to contribute to the household expenses of the family.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It will cause more hardship for the family.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And if the student has to repay study loans, this would also mean a delay in the repayment of the study loan.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, an additional six months' extension of the training period may have different implications on a law student depending on his or her family circumstances.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It may also create the impression that all aspiring lawyers must have deep financial means.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Next, Sir, I want to talk about quality of training.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I recognise that the CPTL wanted to lengthen the training period so as to allow a longer period of mentorship to acquire basic legal skills.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It also allows the mentor lawyer a longer period to assess the trainee lawyer.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Currently, there is no structure for the training contract.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The SILE does provide guidelines but whether the trainee receives proper training very much depends on the law firm and the supervising lawyer.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If a supervising lawyer behaves unethically, then the trainee maybe be learning the wrong behaviour about a lawyer's conduct.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Two years ago, there was a case about a lawyer who took on the role of being a supervising lawyer when he was not qualified to do so.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And according to the judgment by Justice Choo Han Teck, the lawyer may have supervised another trainee who have since been admitted to the Bar.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In other words, that person who had been admitted to the Bar had received training from a supervising lawyer who was not qualified to do so.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Justice Choo had then said in the judgment that the Supervising Authorities should pursue the matter.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, Sir, even if the training contract is for one year and not six months, whether the trainee receives adequate supervision and training during this training period depends very much on the experience and ability of the supervising solicitor.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And even then, the supervising solicitor must have the time to teach or guide the trainee.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Otherwise, the trainee may not benefit from a training contract, whether it is for six months or one year.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Third, Sir, I want to talk about admission of lawyers (NP).

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: My query is on the use of the term "lawyer (NP)".

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Generally, the term "lawyer" is meant to apply to those whose profession is to conduct lawsuits on behalf of clients and to advise as to their legal rights and obligations.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For the non-practising lawyers, they are generally known as legal counsel.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: By adding a category of the term "lawyer (NP)", would members of the public be able to distinguish between a lawyer in active practice and a lawyer (NP) who, in the past would be called a legal counsel?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Would members of the public then feel that lawyers (NP) would be in a position to advise the clients on legal practice matters when they are not really legal practitioners?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But it is important to distinguish the primary function of lawyers and that of legal counsel.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They are separate as they advise different parties.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If so, would there be a large number of applicants because currently, there are many legal counsels who are working in corporate organisations advising their companies.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What would the process be like in dealing with such applications?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: From the Report by the CPTL, I understand that there is an intention to make Part B more vigorous.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I have received a lot of feedback from existing students that the academic workload for Part B is worse than the law school examinations.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I took a look at the course content at the SILE website and I was surprised by the large number of subjects that are covered.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It was as if SILE was trying to squeeze in a few years of legal content into a five- or six-month Part B course.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And that learning journey is always ongoing, because it is impossible to know everything as a lawyer.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The law school examination is meant to give the student academic knowledge of a particular areas of law and the Practice Law Course is to supplement that knowledge in terms of the legal practice.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Otherwise, that person should not have obtained the law degree.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I hope that the Senior Parliamentary Secretary can clarify my queries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: A robust and effective legal system provides a stable environment for our nation's governance and growth and is one of the futures that gives Singapore its ongoing international reputation as a safe, credible and trustworthy country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Lawyers play a vital role in upholding the rule of law, defending rights of individuals and ensuring access to justice for all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The proposal amendments in this Bill align with the recommendations of the CPTL.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The Committee's underlying objectives are to ensure equitable access to professional training for trainee lawyers and to enhance the quality of their training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This guarantees that future lawyers are not technically skilled but are also valued driven and embody compassion, continuous learning, excellence and a commitment to Public Service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The suggested changes aim to foster a legal profession that is both effective and compassionate, with lawyers who carry out their duties guided by principles and accountability and are firmly grounded in ethical practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: With that understanding, while I acknowledge the potential benefits of the changes, I do have some clarifications and suggestions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Before I do so, however, I would like to declare my position as an educator with Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS) and to note that many of the concerns raised in my speech are based on my engagement and discussion with students, university colleagues, legal practitioners and users of Legal Services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that Part B syllabus has been restructured, requiring candidates to complete more modules on different subjects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The expansion in the number of subjects in Part B syllabus reflects a commitment to providing a comprehensive legal education to qualified persons aspiring to practise law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It also acknowledges that the law is a multi-faceted field, touching on various aspects of society, from business and technology, to constitutional rights and environmental concerns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By offering a broader range of subjects, candidates will gain a broader perspective of the law and its intersection with other disciplines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, this broad-based approach needs to be considered in tandem with the practicality of the teaching methodology and the opportunity to observe all this new information.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Though most candidates appreciate the opportunity to learn and be exposed to a variety of subjects, we need to maintain our focus on the critical skills required for candidates to become competent lawyers and be cautious of knowledge overload.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In light of this, could be review the subjects offered in Part B and consider allowing candidates to select courses in areas of their interests.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Doing so could assist to manage knowledge overload while still providing candidates with the opportunity to develop critical skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: On that note and in the context of our national emphasis on lifelong learning, could candidates, once admitted, have the option to select certain broad-based courses as part of their ongoing professional development?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Related, I would like to share that several candidates completing Part B course have commented that they would welcome greater interaction and engagement with senior lawyers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Accordingly, could we explore the possibility of providing mentorship and guidance for candidates at an earlier stage of their Part B education, similar to the Law Society mentorship scheme and in that scheme, supports junior lawyers with less than five years of experience?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It ensures that junior lawyers begin their legal career with a robust foundation, practical experience and a comprehensive grasp of the law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, it benefits law firms by enabling a thorough assessment of their trainees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: He has indicated the longer duration of the practice training period makes it financially onerous for him to pursue a career as a practising lawyer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In addressing the financial challenges and, at the same juncture, to qualify to be called to the Bar, would the Ministry consider offering legal executive positions in public organisations, like the Legal Aid Bureau, Community Law Centre and the Public Defender's Office?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is reassuring that the practice training period can be carried out within pre-approved in-house legal departments or qualified organisations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This offers a chance for trainees to gain exposure to a variety of legal practices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: On that note, may I check with the Ministry on the criteria established in defining the work done as part of the in-house legal departments and how do we assess if a trainee is given the opportunity to rotate within the different legal departments or qualified organisations?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I would now like to talk about the proposed introduction of the provisional practising certificates for trainees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I applaud the Ministry for including this option for trainees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This will surely expand the scope of work for the trainees and strengthen their capabilities in becoming a confident lawyer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that a trainee may receive some allowance while doing similar, if not, the same tasks as an associate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I believe if the current amendment is not accompanied with adjustments to the trainees' allowance, practising as lawyers may become less appealing to new entrants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: On that note, may I check if the Ministry would consider advising law firms to provide a standard package for trainees, including benefits like medical and maternity leave, to ensure a fair and consistent experience for trainee lawyers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to seek clarification on the process for suspension or revocation of provisional practising certificates, and if a trainee does have their professional certificate suspended, are there mandatory causes or relearning procedures for affected trainees?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, I would like to suggest that we provide options for trainees and take into account the unique needs of affected trainees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While law is frequently characterised as being clear-cut, it is essential to acknowledge the diverse characteristics of trainees who are planning to become practising lawyers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We must consider the nuances aspects of law, the various shades of grey when supporting these trainees, without compromising the necessary knowledge and skills to help them achieve their aspiration and goals as competent and responsible lawyers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Considering the potential reduction in the number of contracts offered, will the Ministry encourage law firms to expand their offer of practice training contracts or provide incentives for them to do so?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The legal profession in Singapore plays a pivotal role in preserving peace and justice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Its function in upholding the rule of law, offering access to justice and resolving disputes are essential in guaranteeing the continued fairness and orderliness of the Singaporean society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This may result in fewer lawyers taking on matters related to the needs of the community such as family or criminal law-related cases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is crucial for lawyers to comprehend the challenges their clients face.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Lawyers should actively explore methods for mediation and conflict resolution, when necessary, rather than rushing to push the cases into the courtroom.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This approach helps foster a legal system that is more accessible, empathetic and focused on finding just resolutions for the benefit of all involved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: On that note, is there any consideration for lawyers to receive education on more relational theory of justice such as restorative justice?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: If I may explain, according to the United Nation (UN) Office on Drugs and Crime, and I quote, "restorative justice refers to a way of responding to crime or to the types of wrongdoing, injustice or conflict that focuses primarily on repairing the damage caused by the wrongful action and restoring as in so far as possible the well-being of those involved".

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I believe such topics would enhance the ability of lawyers to provide quality advice aligned to the needs of their clients.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The purpose of lengthening the PTP is to provide trainee lawyers with a longer runway to pick up, grasp and hone their skills to be better lawyers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While the intent is a noble one, this must be balanced against the adverse financial impacts borne by the trainee lawyers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, the financial impact of the prolonged PTP on trainees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Trainee lawyers typically work long hours, from an early start till late into the night and also on weekends.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Some firms offer training contracts with only a pittance as an allowance, which I opine can be seen as exploitative.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This pales in comparison to their peers or fresh graduates in other industries, who draw between S$3,500 or S$5,000, depending on the industry, each month and work lesser hours than these trainees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The trainees are neither less qualified nor less capable than any of their peers in other industries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Indeed, many have gone through rigorous curriculums in the law schools and learnt much in preparation for the law and bar exams.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They have to push on against all odds as they need it to be called to the bar.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And one can say that a new lawyer’s pay goes up significantly upon their call, but the skills and abilities have not suddenly nor exponentially increased.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While I understand that trainee lawyers should not be driven solely by financial rewards, and that the quantum for the monthly honorarium or allowance is largely driven by market forces, it is nonetheless important for them to be paid fairly, in recognition of their skills and contributions to the firms.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The trainees provide valuable contributions to the firm, in terms of research on novel points of the law and preparation of the initial drafts, which are used to advance the client’s case.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To that end, is there more that can be done to ensure our trainees are paid reasonably, especially during the lengthened PTP?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: How can we encourage firms to pay more in terms of the monthly allowance?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: How can the bigger firms also pay more for those on training contracts, as they currently set the de facto upper limit?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: How can we help those from lower-income families, who may need the income to support their families?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the same vein, how can we ensure better retention in the legal industry?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, mandating certain benefits, including paid sick leave, to be provided under training contracts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In my recent interactions with trainees, many have expressed their concerns about the lack of paid sick leave and annual leave, especially with the prolonged PTP period.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: People do fall ill and are required to rest to be more productive.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Apart from COVID-19, there also other strains of flu circulating within our society.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As with all other individuals, trainees also fall ill and may require medical attention from time to time.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Under the existing rules, breaks taken during the PTP will be excluded from the computation of the PTP period.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There is value in such a rule to ensure that trainees complete the entire training period and reap the full benefits of it, and I recognise that.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In view of the above, I am therefore proposing that trainees be accorded paid sick leave when they are unwell, while requiring them to “make-up” for the same number of days at the end of their PTP.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In other words, those who fall ill during the PTP will have an extended PTP – reflecting the “make-up period” – but will be paid a larger allowance or honorarium at the end of the PTP, to reflect the paid sick leave accorded.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Apart from providing trainees with paid sick leave, it may also be useful to let trainees have paid annual leave.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There is a Chinese saying which says " 休息是为了走更远的路 ".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If translated, it means one can accomplish more with adequate rest and breaks along the way.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am really concerned about the overall mental well-being and health of our young trainee lawyers including lawyers in practice.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Any positive move and step can better our workers’ welfare and well-being overall.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Third, training contracts bear some semblance to employment contracts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, the law firm exercises substantial control over the trainee’s work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Apart from training the trainee, the supervising solicitors or other lawyers in the firm set timelines, guide, review and provide input to the trainee’s work before the same is sent to the client for approval.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, the trainee is interviewed by and selected by the law firm, presumably based on the individual’s skills, character and fit, with a view to retain him or her upon the conclusion of the PTP.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This contrasts with a contract for services, whereby a particular vendor is engaged to provide general services.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This includes having access to the firm’s laptop, legal research websites and existing precedents.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Fifth, some of the practice training contracts stipulate the trainee’s working hours and duration, which contrasts with independent contractors who have flexibility over their schedules.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Sixth, the trainee is typically only allowed to work for one employer or law firm at any one point, and should the trainee wish to change firm, he or she must notify SILE beforehand.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is unlike independent contractors who may work for multiple service buyers at the same time.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As the “in-house” option is a popular alternative to private practice, having first-hand experience witnessing the operations and needs of a business would give trainees a flavour of the type of work to expect as an in-house legal counsel.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Additionally, a short stint in companies would help them be more attuned to the business needs of an organisation and consider matters holistically, instead of looking at matters purely from a legal perspective.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I submit that this definition of "corporations" extend to other organisations where they have an in-house team such as NTUC.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With this, it is hoped that they would be more well-rounded lawyers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first set of clarifications relate to the moratorium date on applications for training contracts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill empowers the SILE to disregard any period in calculating the training period completed by a practice trainee.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The explanatory statement clarifies that this may include any contravention of the moratorium date on applications for training contracts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary clarify how any breach of the moratorium date will be factored into calculating the training period completed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, will SILE discount the training period completed by the same amount of time that the practice trainee and law firm breached the moratorium?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would SILE consider certain factors as aggravating or mitigating in this calculation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And are there other penalties that practice trainees would face, apart from the discounting of the training period?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary share whether law firms may face any penalties if they offer practice training contracts in breach of a law student’s moratorium?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It does not appear that this Bill provides for such penalties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If that is the case, can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary explain the rationale behind such an omission?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The omission is odd because the Bill's explanatory statement says that a moratorium is meant to be two-prong: it bars law students from making applications and it bars law practices from making offers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It seems inconsistent and unfair to punish only the student if the law firm wittingly makes an offer in breach of the moratorium date.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Committee for the Professional Training of Lawyers themselves noted in their recommendation that breaches would be hard to detect.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will there be audits or reporting obligations that enable more effective policing of the moratorium?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification is on the exposure of practice trainees to contrasting practice areas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One reason the Committee for the Professional Training of Lawyers (CPTL) recommended increasing the practice training period to one year was to allow practice trainees more meaningful exposures to contrasting practice areas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, small law firms may not be able to provide such exposure, given that their firm's work may be more narrow.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary share what efforts will be made to ensure that even practice trainees in small law firms can have meaningful exposure to different practice areas?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final clarification is on the salary of practice trainees that many Members have raised.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Practice trainees usually receive salaries that are significantly lower than what they would earn as a fully qualified lawyer.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While the media has reported that some law firms are looking to increase practice trainee salaries, relying on individual law firms' review of practice trainees will likely lead to unequal and inequitable outcomes across the board.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While unfortunately some prefer to carelessly put this down to zoomers being not as hungry as those in generations before or feeling less pressure to earn an income, to quote the late and great former Law Society president and unofficial King of Singapore according to LinkedIn, Mr Adrian Tan, "It may be tougher to be a young lawyer now than at any time in history.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They work at an intense pace and are on call night and day." I remember once getting a request from a client to set up a virtual call quickly at about 1.00 am and, on another occasion, leaving the office around 3.00 am after waiting for a turn of documents from the other counsel, only to come back some three hours later to facilitate a deal signing during an auspicious early morning fengshui hour.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, many still want to join the noble profession and numbers grow steadily.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The CPTL was convened in 2016, as shared by many hon Members earlier, to conduct a review of the professional training regime for trainee lawyers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Committee outlined various challenges, including intense competition for practice training contracts, perceived unfair recruitment practices and a lack of consistency in training standards across firms.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Upon the completion of training contracts, the Committee also found the trend of attrition amongst young lawyers due to unsustainable work practices, unsuitability of the individual for legal work and the absence of alternative pathways.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This trend was cast in the spotlight again in 2021.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened by the Government's concern and efforts to work together with industry and schools to improve retention and quality of training.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To quote the International Bar Association (IBA) president, "The young lawyers of today are the senior leaders of tomorrow." I have four clarifications.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, the extension of the practice training period from six to 12 months.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This extension brings us closer to training contracts in some other jurisdictions, for example, 12 months of pupilage in the UK before one practises as a barrister, and 24 months of qualifying work experience in up to four firms for solicitors and 12 months in New South Wales.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The extended timeframe, on one hand, gives trainees more time to oversee cases that cannot be completed in six months and grants firms more time to assess performance for a more informed retention decisions based on mutual fit.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, in my dialogues and engagements with young law students, some have expressed concerns.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given the rising cost of living, coupled with potential debt after university degrees, and another $6,000-plus required for the Part B examinations, some are worried about the quantum of the allowance if the training is lengthened.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In particular, this can be challenging for adult learners or students facing financial challenges.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I, for one, could not have completed my law degree without support from MENDAKI and a Singapore Management University (SMU) scholarship in my first year.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It was only after receiving my first pay cheque as a young lawyer after my training could I finally breathe and contribute to my family after all my parents' sacrifices.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Most law firms also do not charge clients for the work done by trainees.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Should this practice and trend persist with the extension, the current allowance renumerated may not be tenable for trainees and law firms over a long period of time.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In comparison with other jurisdictions, the Law Society in the UK and Bar Standards Board recommend that trainees be paid approximately $2,800 to $3,600 in London.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Furthermore, trainees presently do not have annual or sick leave accounted for during their practice training.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Guidelines under the SILE also necessitate trainees to make up for any leave taken.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This may not be sustainable for the health and well-being of trainees in the long run.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Further, relying on a checklist and increasing the length of the training contract alone may not enrich the quality and rigour of the training experience.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will there be support in place for smaller firms who are unable to cope with the increased costs?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During interactions with young law students, they shared the immense pressure and competition to secure a training contract way ahead of graduation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This practice not only creates additional stress but also questions on whether it is fair to only account for two years of school results in the process.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I would like to clarify on the specific implementation details of the moratorium.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will firms be restricted to only accepting applications in particular months or will students be bound by their year of study for application?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the Ministry enforce this amongst firms upon implementation and what are the avenues for students and firms to voice out any unfair practices that they may observe?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, on the permission for trainees to complete up to three months of the practice training period at approved in-house legal departments of non-law practice entities.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given the broad range of opportunities there are, I can see how this would be an exciting option.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, I was grateful for the chance previously to intern in ESPN, which married my interest in media and the law and helped me understand commercial needs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is there an estimate number of how many of such departments will be available to cater to potential demand?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Council will also be able to direct a lawyer (non-practitioner) to stop practising provisionally until he or she has submitted to a medical examination.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we understand, mental health is a continuum.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government is also generally very cautious about compulsion to submit to medical examinations and the seeking of treatment unless an individual is at risk of harm to themselves or to the public.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are some conditions that will be considered an impairment and how can an individual who has recovered come back to practise?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the changes bring our system closer in alignment to other jurisdictions' standards and guidelines, greater clarity is necessary for aspiring and current law students.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is even more so as the recent changes to the Part B examinations have sparked distress among students.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Previously, students studied seven compulsory subjects and two elective subjects.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also look forward to the future guidance notes, which I understand will be developed in a consultative manner.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond legal practitioners, industry, Government and organisations, I hope that we involve, hear out and co-create with the very people these amendments seek to serve as well – law students themselves.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To do so would be very much in line with the Government's call under Forward SG.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
