text: In her speech, the Senior Parliamentary Secretary also described that many of these guidance notes and subsidiary legislation are in the works.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My final question is whether there is an estimate when these will be ready.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The amendments are a positive development in addressing concerns about the availability of practice roles for our aspiring lawyers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, I have several clarifications on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, there are practical concerns about how this Bill can truly enhance the quality of our legal professionals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, is the supply of training places able to meet the demand?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What trainees do and learn should advance their aspirations and chosen career paths.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, due to a shortage of training positions, a trainee may have little choice but to train at a firm or with a lawyer whose practice areas are vastly different.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: An extended training period may be disadvantageous to them in such cases.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What types of support are available to such trainees if they wish to transition to other practice areas?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, if a trainee is unable to secure a training contract in one of the larger law firms, which may not have as many or as varied legal departments, will there still be an assurance of the same high-quality training?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will these trainees receive the breadth of experience required to enhance their knowledge and skillsets?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can we implement a system, perhaps through logbooks or checklists, to ensure that trainees in smaller law firms, or all trainees, gain the relevant breadth of experience?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This could be a record-keeping document or online system that trainees use to track their activities, experiences and tasks during their practice training period.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Equally important, how do we ensure the accuracy of these logbooks?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Often, larger firms will select those who may have performed better in law school.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does the Law Society ensure that all trainees will continue to get equal exposure, regardless of their graduating results?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, we should consider avenues for trainees to provide anonymous feedback to the Law Society regarding the quality of their training.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This could be an invaluable resource in maintaining and improving the standard of training across the profession in the long term.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Speaker, Sir, as we extend the practice training period, we must be vigilant in safeguarding against the potential exploitation of trainees and their wages.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some firms may take the work of trainees and charge clients as their own without giving due credit to the trainees.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Law Society safeguard against such exploitation?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In such cases, when clients are billed at the full rate, how is liability managed in the event of any issues arising from this arrangement?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Law Society protect those inexperienced trainees from law firms that might seek to take advantage of this extended practice period?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As much as the extended practice period is important to an aspiring lawyer's development, they must also be treated fairly and remunerated equitably.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Addressing the possible exploitation of young lawyers, particularly in larger firms where they are often burdened with arduous tasks and long hours, is critical.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This scenario could also happen in smaller firms where there are fewer resources and manpower.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This unhealthy work environment, characterised by excessive demands and little support, has led to a concerning attrition rate within the profession.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many dedicated individuals have been driven to leave due to these toxic conditions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As with all other occupations, the relationship and balance of power between a supervising solicitor and a trainee tilt in the balance of the former.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Have any measures been put in place to minimise future recurrences?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, it is worth noting that this Bill was crafted during a time when there was an excess of lawyers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Today, we are facing a shortage of legal professionals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Considering this, we must question whether the changes outlined in this Bill remain relevant in our current legal landscape.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Undoubtedly, the quality of our legal professionals is paramount.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Providing them with more time and exposure to different aspects of the legal landscape is a valuable step in their career development.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This, in turn, places more pressure on lawyers, particularly the younger ones, potentially resulting in a vicious cycle as more may experience burnout and leave the profession.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must strike a balance between quality training and ensuring an adequate number of legal professionals to meet the growing demands of our society.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But due to circumstances then, I eventually ended up pursuing Mathematics.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, we need to evaluate the Bill's relevance, considering the evolving legal landscape.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: First, Mr Yip Hon Weng has queried about the relevance of the Bill in our current legal landscape.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: While the Committee's recommendations were made in 2018, they were based on a longer-term, market-neutral perspective.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Earlier, I referred to the recently released Forward SG Report, which stated that Singapore, as a society, wants to recognise and embrace multiple career pathways.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Committee's report in 2018 recognised that the legal profession is a diverse and multi-faceted community with space for persons to contribute in many ways, and that it was important to cater to this.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Committee's recommendations also aimed to ensure overall standards for the professional training of lawyers were lifted.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The existing framework has served Singapore well, training generations of Singapore lawyers who have shaped Singapore's legal industry into the leading legal services hub it is today.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But with the operating environment becoming more complex and competitive, it is even more pressing to adequately prepare our legal workforce for the multitude of roles that they may be expected to play in the future.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Our world is getting smaller yet increasingly polarised, and the lawyers of tomorrow will need to work collaboratively while embracing diversity, as they engage in more cross-border work.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Legal tech is increasingly used by law firms, in-house legal departments, the Courts and dispute resolution institutions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As consumers become more sophisticated, there is also growing demand for higher-value advice from lawyers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As I mentioned earlier, this Bill is part of overall efforts to uplift the quality of law students and better prepare a future-ready legal workforce.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Whether lawyers practise in a big or small Singapore law practice, or SLP, or in an international firm, their employer, clients and the broader industry will benefit from them having a better-grounded foundation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Upon completing their PTP, they will be better equipped to hit the ground running.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Next, I will address questions from Mr Yip and Mr Patrick Tay on whether the recommendations will impact the supply of lawyers in Singapore, including whether there will be adequate practice training places and on retention of aspiring young lawyers in the industry.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The attrition of lawyers is not a new phenomenon.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Lawyers have many different options, aside from private practice.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These include becoming in-house counsel, joining the Government or legal tech companies or entering academia.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Legal talent is required to support all aspects of Singapore's economy and society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Through this Bill, we hope to better equip future law graduates to seize the myriad of opportunities available.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: At the same time, for those who choose to, the changes will better prepare and sustain them through the rigours of legal practice.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked about the need for the new nomenclature of lawyer (NP) and their role in the legal landscape vis-à-vis other legal professionals.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Both he and Mr Raj Joshua Thomas asked if, going forward, in-house legal counsel will need to, first, be admitted as lawyers (NP).

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The nomenclature of "lawyer (non-practitioner)" was determined after public consultation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It was not intended to replace the term "legal counsel", nor was it intended to introduce new qualification requirements for in-house counsel.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Rather, it is to distinguish lawyers (NP) from advocates and solicitors and other individuals, while still recognising them as crucial stakeholders in the legal industry.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The nomenclature does not reflect any professional hierarchy; it differentiates who is able to practise in the public's and industry's minds.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For existing in-house legal counsel who wish to be admitted as lawyers (NP), this would depend on whether they fall within the transitional arrangements in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Next, several Members, including Mr Louis Ng and Ms Nadia Samdin raised questions relating to the content and quality of the practice training during the lengthened Practice Training Period, or PTP.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On this, I earlier mentioned that the SILE has published a detailed notice on its website outlining the new training requirements.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Some of these requirements are already found in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This includes the Legal Profession (Admission) Rules 2011, or the Admission Rules, which already provide for the responsibilities of supervising solicitors and training SLPs under practice training contracts; how a practice trainee may serve his or her PTP, including in certain law offices in the Public Service, such as the Public Defender's Office; and flexibility for practice trainees to undertake their practice training with more than one SLP.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This recognises that training SLPs may not have the expertise or resources to provide exposure to all the required practice areas.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The door is also open for trainees to provide feedback on their training.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Law Society has a dedicated email address and the Members' Assistance and Care Helpline through which it offers career counselling, mentorship, guidance and practical tips to members and law graduates who are seeking to practise law.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Several Members have raised the issue of honoraria and leave benefits for practice trainees during the lengthened PTP.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Concerns include whether practice trainees are being treated as "cheap" labour; whether during the lengthened PTP, practice trainees from lower-income families or who have additional responsibilities, will face a disproportionate or undue financial burden; and whether practice trainees will "burn out" if they are not given leave benefits.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As part of the plan to implement the Committee's recommendations, we have been discussing measures to address them with the working groups.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I will, first, cover the issue of honoraria.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Practice training is, at its core, an apprenticeship, where aspiring legal practitioners seek out mentors to guide them in the industry and provide opportunities for practical exposure.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is a symbiotic relationship, where both trainees and supervising solicitors come together to contribute to the continued development of Singapore's legal industry.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Through the mentorship and experience gained from being attached to a supervising solicitor, a practice trainee is better equipped to operate independently as a lawyer.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Training SLPs are often a practice trainee's first taste of legal practice and its accompanying realities and rigours.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As ambassadors of the legal industry, it is important for training SLPs and supervising solicitors to support trainees, through the transition from school to legal practice with understanding, patience and fairness.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This also sets the tone for a potentially longer-term employment relationship in the foreseeable future.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We encourage training SLPs to provide fair and reasonable honoraria that recognises trainees' contributions and allows them to meet their financial obligations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Under the new framework, training SLPs could also choose to grant larger honoraria to trainees with provisional PCs, recognising that they undertake a broader scope of responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: At the same time, we recognise that this needs to be balanced against the potential increased costs to law practices, particularly the smaller SLPs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: At present, there is no legislation prohibiting training SLPs from charging out for trainees' work.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Law Society has released guidance on such charging, which could help defray some costs of a longer PTP.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Charging out for trainees' work would also recognise trainees' contributions and engender a greater sense of belonging within the profession.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: That said, training SLPs will have to be mindful that charging clients for work done by practice trainees may change the nature of their relationship with the trainee to that of an employment relationship, with attendant CPF and employment tax obligations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Some Members have suggested mandating a minimum honorarium quantum.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The quantum also risks being set above what some small SLPs can afford and may also have the inadvertent effect of reducing the number of training places offered.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: MinLaw and the Law Society will continue to monitor the industry trends.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Next, I will address the issue of leave benefits.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: More details will be announced in due course.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Beyond pay and leave, we also recognise that there are other important factors in ensuring a trainee's mental well-being.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Law Society has led by example by establishing the Law Society Mentorship Scheme and the Young Lawyers Law Mentor Scheme.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These schemes provide platforms for law graduates and young lawyers to discuss issues on mental well-being, career development and ethics in full confidentiality with more experienced mentors.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Next, Mr Murali Pillai sought clarification on the length of PTP that legal and judicial service officers, or LSOs and JSOs, will be required to complete under the new framework.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum had also asked about completing PTP within the Public Service.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Today, LSOs and JSOs who wish to be admitted to the Bar can do so after completing their PTP, which is currently 36 months.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: However, unlike their peers in private practice, LSOs and JSOs are not required to be admitted to the Bar to perform their job functions in the Public Service.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Their progression is also not prejudiced or affected by admission to the Bar.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Trainees may continue to complete their PTP by working as an LSO or a JSO, or under the supervision of a Qualifying Relevant Legal Officer in the public sector.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: A review was undertaken of the training programme for LSOs and JSOs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Committee's report noted that there is little substantive difference in the content or quality of training provided in the public and private sectors.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In both cases, the training covers legal skills, professional responsibilities and ethics, etiquette and conduct.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This was a key rationale for the change in the PTP period for LSOs and JSOs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Next, several Members raised questions and concerns about implementing the CPTL's recommendation to raise the standards and stringency of the Part B Bar exams.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This topic falls outside the scope of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This was one of the Committee's key structural recommendations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It was intended to ensure that the quality of the Singapore Bar remains consistently high and to better equip our law graduates.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: SILE has revamped the Part B Course to include topics that are gaining importance, focus on core principles and mirror the realities of practice.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: SILE has received constructive feedback from the industry and current candidates.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Support has been offered to the current candidates, including more on-demand video lectures and contact hours, live Q&A segments during Contact Sessions and recordings for candidates to review.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: MinLaw will continue working with SILE to engage current candidates to understand where the gaps are and what further refinements can be introduced.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Next, on allowing up to three months of PTP to be completed at the in-house legal departments of approved non-law practice entities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Members had asked for more details about the application process, the qualifying criteria for these entities and had proposed entities for consideration.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The working group will refer to these proposed criteria and Members' suggestions when preparing the subsidiary legislation on the qualifying criteria.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Non-law practice entities that wish to offer training opportunities may write to SILE and MinLaw to register their interest in being considered.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Some Members asked about how the new framework for provisional PCs will be operationalised, such as the professional indemnity insurance requirements, what happens if a provisional PC is suspended or revoked and how a lawyer (NP)'s fitness to hold a provisional PC will be determined.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I had mentioned in my opening speech that the framework for provisional PCs in the Bill is substantively similar to that concerning PCs for advocates and solicitors.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is, therefore, open to the relevant stakeholders to take guidance from existing practices and case law concerning PCs, such as a solicitor's fitness to hold a PC when applying the new provisional PC framework.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Further operational details are being worked on by the multi-stakeholder working groups and will be released in due course.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Next, several Members have sought clarification on how the moratorium period will be implemented and operationalised, including how breaches will be detected and possible consequences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The multi-stakeholder working group has been discussing these details.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As mentioned earlier, this Bill amends the Act to provide flexibility for implementing such details in the future.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Before introducing the measures to strictly enforce the moratorium period, the relevant agencies will engage law students and law practices to socialise the change.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Several Members have also raised issues not directly covered in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These touch on implementation and operational details of the Committee's recommendations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, the relationship between trainees and supervising solicitors, suggestions for Continuing Professional Development activities and the extension of the SkillsFuture Mid-Career Enhanced Subsidy to support trainees during the lengthened PTP.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: MinLaw will work with the relevant stakeholders and working groups to review the feedback received.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do Members have any clarifications for Senior Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu?
